title: Perinatal mental health
blurb: Screen, refer and treat mental health problems in pregnancy and the year after birth using NICE CG192.
question: Grace gave birth 6 days ago. She has bipolar disorder. Her partner phones the community mental health team: since last night she has not slept, is talking rapidly about the baby being 'chosen' and seems confused. What should the nurse do?

teach.h: The perinatal period: higher stakes for two
teach.body: Perinatal mental health covers pregnancy and the first year after birth. NICE CG192 (Antenatal and postnatal mental health) asks every professional to look for depression and anxiety, which are under-recognised at this time, and to act fast on severe illness. Women may not disclose symptoms through fear of stigma or of their baby being taken into care (CG192 1.5.1). Plain English: ask kindly, ask routinely, and treat a sudden change after birth as urgent.

teach.h: Screening at booking and early postnatal (CG192 1.5.4-1.5.6)

steps.label: 2 Whooley questions
steps.sub: Low mood; loss of interest, past month

steps.label: GAD-2
steps.sub: Nervous or on edge; can't stop worrying, past 2 weeks

steps.label: Whooley positive
steps.sub: EPDS or PHQ-9, or refer to GP

steps.label: Severe illness suspected
steps.sub: Refer to a mental health professional

teach.caption: Consider asking both again at all later contacts in pregnancy and the first year (1.5.8).

Refer anyone with current or past severe mental illness to secondary (ideally specialist perinatal) mental health services and tell the GP (1.5.10).

teach.body: Grace has bipolar disorder and, on day 6, sudden sleeplessness, pressured speech, a delusional belief about her baby and confusion. This is suspected postpartum psychosis, a psychiatric emergency. The nurse arranges immediate assessment by the specialist perinatal or crisis team, within 4 hours of referral, advises her partner that Grace should not be left alone with the baby until assessed, and plans for admission to a mother and baby unit if inpatient care is needed.

teach.text: Do not file sudden confusion or odd beliefs in the first weeks after birth under 'baby blues' or 'just tired'. Blues are mild tearfulness that settles within about 2 weeks; psychosis is sudden, severe and urgent. And remember CG192 pairs the Whooley questions WITH the GAD-2: screening asks about anxiety as well as depression.

items: Booking and early postnatal: 2 Whooley questions plus GAD-2; consider again at later contacts.
Whooley positive: EPDS or PHQ-9, or GP. GAD-2 score 3 or more: GAD-7 or GP.
Suspected postpartum psychosis: assessment within 4 hours; mother and baby unit within 12 months of birth.
No valproate in pregnancy; lithium only if antipsychotics fail; breastfeeding encouraged unless on carbamazepine, clozapine or lithium.

summary: You can now screen for perinatal depression and anxiety with the Whooley questions and GAD-2 and act on the results. You can also recognise postpartum psychosis as an emergency and apply CG192 advice on medicines in pregnancy and breastfeeding.

A.q: At a booking appointment the midwife asks the two Whooley questions. Which further brief tool does NICE CG192 suggest asking at the same contact?
options: The AUDIT-C questionnaire
The GAD-2 anxiety questions
The Mini-Mental State Examination
The full 21-item Beck inventory
A.why: CG192 1.5.4: at booking and in the early postnatal period, consider the 2 depression identification (Whooley) questions and also the GAD-2 to ask about anxiety.

whyNot.0: AUDIT is used if alcohol misuse is suspected (1.5.13), not alongside every Whooley screen.
whyNot.2: The MMSE is a cognitive test, not a perinatal mood screen.
whyNot.3: CG192 does not name the Beck inventory for screening.

A.q: A woman scores 4 on the GAD-2 at her 10-day postnatal visit. What does NICE CG192 advise?
options: Repeat the GAD-2 at her 6-week check
Refer directly for inpatient admission
Use the GAD-7 or refer her to her GP
Start a short course of a benzodiazepine
A.why: CG192 1.5.6: a GAD-2 score of 3 or more means considering the GAD-7 for further assessment or referring to the GP (or a mental health professional if severe illness is suspected).

whyNot.0: A positive screen needs further assessment now, not a delayed repeat.
whyNot.1: Nothing suggests severe illness requiring admission.
whyNot.3: Benzodiazepines are only for short-term severe anxiety and agitation, after assessment.

A.q: Within what time does NICE CG192 expect assessment after referral for suspected postpartum psychosis?
options: Within 4 hours
Within 24 hours
Within 72 hours
Within 2 weeks
A.why: CG192 1.5.12: sudden onset of symptoms suggesting postpartum psychosis needs immediate assessment, within 4 hours of referral.

whyNot.1: 24 hours is too slow for a psychiatric emergency.
whyNot.2: 72 hours is not the CG192 standard.
whyNot.3: 2 weeks is the standard for routine perinatal referrals (1.7.3).

B.q: Fatima, 3 days after birth, is tearful and feels overwhelmed but sleeps when the baby sleeps, is caring well for her baby and has no unusual beliefs. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Postpartum psychosis needing assessment in 4 hours
Moderate postnatal depression needing an SSRI
Baby blues, which usually settle within 2 weeks
Generalised anxiety disorder needing a GAD-7 today
B.why: Brief tearfulness in the first days without psychotic features or severe low mood fits the baby blues, which usually go within 2 weeks; she should still be supported and reviewed.

whyNot.0: There are no psychotic features, confusion or sudden severe change.
whyNot.1: Depression needs persistent symptoms; this is day 3 with mild emotional changes.
whyNot.3: Nothing here suggests persistent, uncontrollable worry.

B.q: Leah, 28, takes valproate for bipolar disorder and finds she is 7 weeks pregnant. What does NICE CG192 advise?
options: Continue valproate at the lowest dose
Stop valproate because of fetal risk
Switch to carbamazepine straight away
Continue until the second trimester
B.why: CG192 1.4.29: if a woman taking valproate becomes pregnant, stop the drug because of the risk of fetal malformations and adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes; specialist advice on alternatives follows.

whyNot.0: Valproate is stopped in pregnancy, not reduced.
whyNot.2: CG192 also advises against carbamazepine in pregnancy (1.4.30).
whyNot.3: Continuing exposes the fetus to further risk.

B.q: A woman with schizophrenia stable on clozapine asks about breastfeeding her baby. What does NICE CG192 say?
options: Breastfeed and have the baby monitored weekly
Breastfeed after halving the clozapine dose
Breastfeed once her clozapine level is checked
It is not encouraged while taking clozapine
B.why: CG192 1.9.8: encourage women with a mental health problem to breastfeed unless they take carbamazepine, clozapine or lithium; support her choice of feeding method.

whyNot.0: Clozapine is a named exception to encouraging breastfeeding.
whyNot.1: Halving the dose risks relapse and does not make breastfeeding advised.
whyNot.2: A plasma level does not change the CG192 position.

C.q: Sofia continues lithium through pregnancy because she relapsed on antipsychotics. She is now 37 weeks. What monitoring does NICE CG192 advise?
options: Lithium levels weekly, birth in hospital
Lithium levels monthly, home birth possible
Lithium levels every 4 weeks until birth
Stop lithium at 36 weeks, restart after birth
C.why: CG192 1.4.37: check plasma lithium every 4 weeks, then weekly from 36 weeks; keep fluid balance; birth in hospital; stop lithium in labour and check the level 12 hours after the last dose.

whyNot.1: Monitoring becomes weekly from 36 weeks and birth should be in hospital.
whyNot.2: Four-weekly checks change to weekly from the 36th week.
whyNot.3: Lithium is stopped during labour, not routinely at 36 weeks.

C.q: Rosa, 9 months postnatal, has severe depression with suicidal thoughts and needs inpatient care. She wants to keep caring for her baby. Where should she normally be admitted?
options: An adult acute ward, with the baby cared for by family
A specialist mother and baby unit
A paediatric ward with her baby
A general medical ward for observation
C.why: CG192 1.10.1: women who need inpatient mental health care within 12 months of childbirth should normally be admitted to a specialist mother and baby unit.

whyNot.0: Separation is not the default within 12 months of birth.
whyNot.2: Paediatric wards care for sick children, not maternal mental illness.
whyNot.3: A medical ward cannot provide specialist perinatal care.

C.q: At booking, Mei answers 'no' to both Whooley questions and scores 1 on the GAD-2, but says she now avoids supermarkets and buses. What should the midwife do next under NICE CG192?
options: Record a negative screen and recheck after birth
Ask about avoidance; consider GAD-7 or GP referral
Complete the EPDS to rule out depression first
Refer urgently to the perinatal crisis team today
C.why: CG192 1.5.7: with a GAD-2 score under 3 but continuing concern, ask whether she avoids places or activities and whether this causes problems; if yes, consider GAD-7 or GP referral.

whyNot.0: Clinical concern remains, so CG192 asks a further avoidance question.
whyNot.2: The EPDS follows a positive depression screen; her concern is anxiety.
whyNot.3: Nothing suggests severe illness needing crisis care.

reteach.title: Two screens, one urgent red flag
reteach.question: What must every perinatal contact include?

blocks.h: Depression AND anxiety, then watch for psychosis
blocks.body: At booking and early postnatal: ask the 2 Whooley questions (depression) and the GAD-2 (anxiety). A 'yes' to Whooley leads to EPDS or PHQ-9 or a GP referral; GAD-2 of 3 or more leads to GAD-7 or a GP referral. Separately, in the first 2 weeks after birth, watch women with SMI or a family history closely: sudden psychosis needs assessment within 4 hours.

blocks.text: GAD-2 threshold is 3, not 'any yes'. Whooley is positive with any yes.

explain.body: During the past month, have you often been bothered by feeling down, depressed or hopeless? And by having little interest or pleasure in doing things? A yes to either leads to further assessment.

test.q: A pregnant woman answers yes to one Whooley question. What does NICE CG192 advise considering?
options: EPDS or PHQ-9 as part of a full assessment
No action unless both questions are positive
An urgent same-day psychiatric admission
Repeating both questions at the 36-week visit
test.why: CG192 1.5.5: a positive response to either question means considering the EPDS or PHQ-9 as part of a full assessment, or referral to the GP.

whyNot.1: A yes to either question is a positive screen.
whyNot.2: Admission is not indicated by a positive screen alone.

explain.body: Two questions over the last 2 weeks: feeling nervous, anxious or on edge; not being able to stop or control worrying. Each scores 0 to 3. Score 3 or more: GAD-7 or GP.

test.q: Which GAD-2 total score should prompt a GAD-7 or GP referral under NICE CG192?
options: A score of 1 or more
A score of 2 or more
A score of 5 or more
A score of 3 or more
test.why: CG192 1.5.6: a GAD-2 score of 3 or more prompts the GAD-7 or GP referral.

whyNot.2: Waiting for 5 would miss women at the threshold of 3 or 4.

explain.body: Sudden onset, usually within 2 weeks of birth: mania, delusions, confusion. Be alert in women with SMI or a first-degree family history. Refer for assessment within 4 hours.

test.q: Which woman does NICE CG192 say needs particular alertness for postpartum psychosis in the first 2 weeks after birth?
options: A woman with a past episode of baby blues
A woman whose mother had postpartum psychosis
A woman who had a caesarean birth
A woman who is formula feeding her baby
test.why: CG192 1.5.11: be alert if there is past or present severe mental illness or severe perinatal mental illness in a first-degree relative.

whyNot.0: Baby blues is not a severe mental illness.
whyNot.2: Mode of birth is not the CG192 trigger.
whyNot.3: Feeding method is not a named risk factor.

explain.body: Higher threshold for drugs in pregnancy; lowest effective dose, single drug. No valproate; lithium only if antipsychotics fail; benzodiazepines only short-term for severe anxiety. Breastfeeding encouraged except with carbamazepine, clozapine or lithium.

test.q: A pregnant woman with severe anxiety is prescribed a benzodiazepine. Which use fits NICE CG192?
options: Long-term use throughout pregnancy
Use until breastfeeding is established
Short-term use for severe anxiety and agitation
Regular use as a first-line treatment
test.why: CG192 1.4.18: do not offer benzodiazepines in pregnancy and the postnatal period except for short-term treatment of severe anxiety and agitation.

whyNot.1: CG192 advises considering gradually stopping benzodiazepines if breastfeeding.
